desc:
An undirected tree has n nodes numbered 0..n-1 and n - 1 edges [a, b]. The distance between two nodes is the number of edges on the unique path connecting them.

Return the number of unordered pairs of distinct nodes {u, v} whose distance is exactly k.

n = 6, edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[1,3],[1,4],[2,5]], k = 2

pairs: {0,3} {0,4} {0,5} {3,4} {1,2}   -> 5
constraints: edges.length = n - 1 and the edges form a tree
hints: A BFS from every node counts everything but costs O(n<sup>2</sup>) overall. Use the fact that k is small.

Root the tree. For every node v let cnt[v][d] be the number of nodes at depth d below v (d from 0 to k). A pair at distance k has a top node (their lowest common ancestor) at which the two halves meet.

Merge the children of v one by one into cnt[v]. Before adding a child c, every node already collected at depth i can pair with every node at depth k - 1 - i below c; add cur[i] * cnt[c][k-1-i], then fold c's counts in, shifted by one.
editorial: Every pair of nodes has a unique lowest common ancestor in the rooted tree, so count each pair at its LCA. Keep, for each node, an array cnt[d] for d = 0..k: the number of nodes in its subtree at depth exactly d below it (so cnt[0] = 1).

Process nodes bottom-up. For a node v start with cur = [1, 0, ..., 0] (just v). For each child c in turn, count the pairs that have v as LCA and one node inside c's subtree and the other either v itself or inside an earlier child's subtree: for each i, cur[i] * cnt[c][k - 1 - i], because a node at depth j below c is at depth j + 1 below v and we need i + j + 1 = k. Then add c into cur: cur[j+1] += cnt[c][j]. Merging children one at a time ensures that nodes from the same child are never paired through v.

Each merge costs O(k), and there are n - 1 merges, so the total time is O(n · k). The answer is at most n(n-1)/2 ≤ 1.25 · 10<sup>9</sup>, which fits in 32 bits. Use an iterative bottom-up order to avoid deep recursion.
